explanation: The hypothesis addresses corrosion resistance in application-relevant stainless steels and proposes a testable chromium-passivation mechanism, but it does not reconstruct the target study. It substitutes severe-plastic-deformation-induced ultrafine grains in bulk 304/duplex steel for an atmospheric-plasma-sprayed AlCoCrFeNi coating on SS316L annealed at 550 °C. Consequently, the processing parameters, grain scale, phases, exposure media, and principal hot-corrosion conditions do not agree with the target. There is limited mechanistic overlap through grain refinement and Cr-rich passive-film formation, and the predicted reductions in corrosion current and pitting are directionally consistent with part of the target outcome. The controlled same-batch comparison, surface-film characterization, electrochemistry, and explicit falsification rule make the alternative experimentally useful. However, HPT simultaneously changes residual stress, defect density, texture, and possibly phase distribution, so the proposed two-group study cannot uniquely attribute an improvement to grain-boundary-assisted chromium diffusion; recovery/annealing controls or matched-defect controls would improve discrimination. E3 directly supports improved passivation and chromium enrichment in UFG stainless steels, while the other evidence appropriately indicates environmental and microgalvanic limitations. Evidence for extension to 320 °C pressurized-water-reactor conditions is not directly supplied. The idea is scientifically plausible but already established in the cited review, limiting novelty.
